A.explanation: Loading and unloading follow the same straight line back to the origin, so extension is zero when force is zero with no permanent set.

B.explanation: Loading and unloading follow the same curved path back to the origin, so the deformation is elastic and non-linear with no permanent extension.

C.explanation: Unloading follows a different path but still returns to zero extension at zero force, which is elastic hysteresis as in rubber, not permanent plastic set.

D.explanation: Unloading follows a line that meets the extension axis above zero, so a residual extension remains when force is zero, which is plastic deformation.

hints: Notice the arrows for increasing force and decreasing force on each force-extension graph and check where each unloading curve meets the axes.
Recall that plastic deformation means permanent extension remains when the force is removed, so the unloading line must intercept the extension axis at a value greater than zero.
Compare the loops that return to the origin with the one that leaves extension at zero force to decide which shows a permanent set.
walkthrough: Look at what each graph plots: force on the vertical axis against extension on the horizontal axis, with arrows showing loading as force increases and unloading as force decreases.
State the test for plastic behaviour: if the material is plastically deformed, unloading to $F = 0$ leaves $x > 0$, a permanent extension.
Check graphs A and B: the unloading arrow retraces the loading curve back to the origin, so $x = 0$ when $F = 0$ and the deformation is elastic.
Check graph C: unloading takes a lower path forming a hysteresis loop, but it still finishes at the origin, so $x = 0$ when $F = 0$ and there is no permanent set.
Check the remaining graph: loading is initially linear then curves, and unloading is an approximately straight line that intercepts the extension axis at a positive extension when force is zero.
That residual extension at zero force is the signature of plastic deformation. This is option D.
